In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the low-angle normal fault system and the associated dike swarm were formed in a complex, multistage extensional tectonic regime in which the regional stress field changed in orientation and intensity, and in which the local stress field was modified by flexural warping and isostatic uplift of the lower crustal plate.

the low-angle normal fault systems and associated dike emplacement in the Homer, Newberry, Sacramento, and Dead Mountain region were the result of a complex interplay of extensional, contractional, and isostatic processes.
the Homer Mountain area was a region of low-angle extensional faulting in a zone of regional east-northeastwest-southwest crust extension.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

low-angle normal faults, dike swarms, and associated volcanic and sedimentary deposits record the middle Miocene history of extensional tectonism in the western part of the lower Colorado River basin.
low-angle faulting and associated dikes are a regional phenomenon, but the geometry of the faults and the orientation of the dikes are not necessarily regional.
low-angle faulting in the upper plate and dike em placement in the lower plate occurred in response to a combination of regional crustal extension and local subhorizontal compression.
The main takeaway from our work is that
low-angle faulting in the Homer Mountain area is not related to regional crustal extension, but instead is related to crustal compression.
low-angle faulting and diabase emplacement in the lower crust are intimately linked, and that low-angle normal fault zones may provide pathways for diabase emplacement at shallow crustal depths.
